title: Self-testing Quantum Supermaps
authors: Victor Barizien, Cyril Branciard, Alastair A. Abbott, Jean-Daniel Bancal, Pavel Sekatski
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By certifying quantum operations from measurement statistics directly, without any assumption on the internal workings of the devices involved, self-testing enables a uniquely reliable identification of quantum objects. While such device-independent characterization has been shown to be possible for states, measurements and channels, it has so far not been extended to quantum supermaps -- operations that act on quantum channels themselves and can combine them in either a well-defined causal order or also, remarkably, in an indefinite causal order. Here we show that quantum supermaps can be identified device-independently. Specifically, we obtain two levels of certification, depending on the network structure of the experiment: when each slot of the supermap accepts a single uncharacterized black box, identification up to local embedding combs is obtained; when several black boxes are inserted within each slot, identification up to local extracting and injecting maps is achieved. We illustrate our approach on four examples -- the identity comb, a bit-flip error-correcting comb, the comb describing Grover's algorithm, and the quantum switch -- providing in particular the first self-test of both a quantum algorithmic comb and a causally indefinite quantum process. Notably, in the latter case, this provides a new way to certify causal indefiniteness in a device-independent manner.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum supermaps can be self-tested device-independently, providing the first self-tests of a quantum algorithmic comb and a causally indefinite process.
motivation: Self-testing has been extended to states, measurements, and channels, but not to quantum supermaps, which are essential for quantum algorithms and indefinite causal order. Certifying supermaps device-independently would enable reliable identification of complex quantum operations.
method: The authors develop two levels of certification depending on the network structure: when each slot accepts a single black box, identification up to local embedding combs; when multiple black boxes are inserted per slot, identification up to local extracting and injecting maps. They apply this to four examples including the quantum switch.
result: They achieve device-independent self-testing of quantum supermaps, demonstrating certification of the identity comb, a bit-flip error-correcting comb, Grover's algorithm comb, and the quantum switch, the latter providing a new way to certify causal indefiniteness.
conclusion: Quantum supermaps can be identified device-independently, extending self-testing to a broader class of quantum operations and enabling new protocols for certifying indefinite causal order.

The approach is illustrated on four examples: the identity comb, a bit-flip error-correcting comb, the comb describing Grover's algorithm, and the quantum switch. Notably, this provides the first self-test of both a quantum algorithmic comb and a causally indefinite quantum process, offering a new way to certify causal indefiniteness in a device-independent manner.

title: Quantum Conditional Mutual Information And Channel Capacity
authors: D. -S. Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Information measures acquire operational meaning through coding theorems. The quantum conditional mutual information (QCMI) is nonnegative due to strong subadditivity, yet a direct connection with channel coding has remained elusive. In this work, we propose a quantum communication task-conditional quantum communication-that fills this gap. We show that the optimal rate for establishing quantum correlation between two parties, assisted by a third system, is given by half the QCMI. This result naturally extends the classical key generation capacity of Csisz\'ar and Ahlswede to the quantum domain. We place our model within the family tree of quantum protocols and compute the conditional capacity for several example channels. Our results provide new insights for code design in reliable quantum information processing.
tldr: Establishes the quantum conditional mutual information as the optimal rate for conditional quantum communication, extending classical key generation capacity to the quantum domain.
motivation: The quantum conditional mutual information (QCMI) lacked a direct operational interpretation in channel coding, despite its fundamental role in quantum information theory.
method: Proposes a new communication task—conditional quantum communication—and proves that the optimal rate for establishing quantum correlation between two parties assisted by a third is half the QCMI, using coding theorems and information-theoretic arguments.
result: The optimal rate for conditional quantum communication is given by half the quantum conditional mutual information, and the conditional capacity is computed for several example channels.
conclusion: This work provides a direct operational meaning for QCMI, linking it to channel capacity and offering new insights for code design in quantum information processing.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper establishes a direct operational interpretation of the quantum conditional mutual information (QCMI) in terms of a communication task called conditional quantum communication. The authors propose a scenario where two parties, Alice and Bob, aim to establish quantum correlation (entanglement) with the assistance of a third system held by Charlie. They prove that the optimal rate at which they can generate shared quantum correlation is exactly half the QCMI of the underlying quantum state. This result generalizes the classical key generation capacity of Csiszár and Ahlswede to the quantum setting, providing a quantum analogue of the classical result that the conditional mutual information characterizes the rate of secret key agreement. The paper also places the proposed model within the broader family of quantum protocols, such as state merging and quantum channel coding, and computes the conditional capacity for several example channels, including the erasure channel and the dephasing channel.
key_contributions: Introduces the task of conditional quantum communication, providing an operational meaning for the quantum conditional mutual information.
Proves that the optimal rate for establishing quantum correlation assisted by a third party is half the QCMI, extending classical key generation results to the quantum domain.
Places the new protocol within the existing family of quantum information protocols, clarifying its relationship to state merging and quantum channel coding.
Computes the conditional capacity for specific quantum channels (e.g., erasure, dephasing), demonstrating the utility of the result.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs information-theoretic methods typical in quantum Shannon theory. The main approach is to define a protocol for conditional quantum communication, where Alice and Bob share a quantum state with Charlie, and they aim to distill entanglement using local operations and classical communication (LOCC) with Charlie's assistance. The achievability part uses a quantum version of the Csiszár-Körner strategy, involving random coding and typical subspace arguments. The converse is derived from the quantum data processing inequality and the monotonicity of the QCMI under local operations. The proof techniques are rigorous and rely on established tools such as the quantum asymptotic equipartition property and the decoupling theorem. The paper also provides a clear operational interpretation by connecting the QCMI to the rate of entanglement generation, which is a natural quantum generalization of classical key agreement.
deep_read.results_analysis: The central result is that the conditional quantum communication capacity, defined as the maximum rate of entanglement generation between Alice and Bob with Charlie's help, equals half the QCMI of the state shared among all three parties. For example, for a pure tripartite state, the QCMI reduces to the conditional entropy, and the capacity becomes half the conditional entropy. The paper computes explicit capacities for the erasure channel (where the QCMI is given by the erasure probability) and the dephasing channel (where the QCMI depends on the dephasing parameter). These examples illustrate that the capacity can be nonzero even when the direct channel between Alice and Bob is noisy, highlighting the role of Charlie as a helper. The results are consistent with known special cases, such as when Charlie's system is trivial, the capacity reduces to the entanglement of formation.
strengths: Provides a long-sought operational interpretation of the quantum conditional mutual information, which is a fundamental quantity in quantum information theory.
The result is elegant and general, unifying classical and quantum information theory by extending the Csiszár-Ahlswede theorem.
The paper is well-structured, with clear definitions and rigorous proofs, making it accessible to researchers in the field.
Includes concrete examples that demonstrate the applicability of the result to realistic quantum channels.
limitations: The analysis assumes asymptotic i.i.d. scenarios; finite-size effects and practical implementation issues are not addressed.
The protocol requires Charlie to be a trusted helper; the security implications in adversarial settings are not considered.
The capacity formula involves half the QCMI, which may be challenging to compute for general quantum states due to the optimization over extensions.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and information theory by providing a fundamental operational interpretation of the quantum conditional mutual information. It bridges classical and quantum information theory, offering new insights into quantum correlations and channel coding. The results are relevant for understanding the role of quantum entanglement in communication and for designing quantum protocols that leverage auxiliary systems. The result is novel, technically sound, and elegantly connects classical and quantum results. It is a high-quality work that merits strong attention from the quantum information community.

title: A Gauge-Theoretic Formulation Of Nambu Non-equilibrium Thermodynamics
authors: So Katagiri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a gauge-theoretic formulation of Nambu non-equilibrium thermodynamics (NNET). In this framework, the thermodynamic potential [MATH] plays the role of a gauge field: the reversible thermodynamics corresponds to the pure-gauge condition [MATH], while the irreversible entropy production arises from the emergence of curvature [MATH]. The gauge-fixing term, [MATH] leads to Onsager's variational principle, whereas the Chern--Simons--like term [MATH] naturally yields the framework of NNET. This formulation provides a unified geometric foundation for both reversible and irreversible processes in thermodynamics.
tldr: A gauge-theoretic formulation of non-equilibrium thermodynamics using Nambu brackets, unifying reversible and irreversible processes via curvature.
motivation: To provide a unified geometric foundation for both reversible and irreversible thermodynamics, extending Nambu mechanics to non-equilibrium settings.
method: The thermodynamic potential is treated as a gauge field; reversible dynamics corresponds to pure-gauge condition, while irreversible entropy production emerges from curvature. Gauge-fixing yields Onsager's principle, and a Chern-Simons-like term gives Nambu non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
result: The framework naturally reproduces Onsager's variational principle and Nambu non-equilibrium thermodynamics, offering a geometric perspective on entropy production.
conclusion: This gauge-theoretic approach provides a novel, unified geometric foundation for non-equilibrium thermodynamics, potentially enabling new insights into irreversible processes.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a gauge-theoretic formulation of Nambu non-equilibrium thermodynamics (NNET), where the thermodynamic potential A_i = ∂_i S is interpreted as a gauge field. Reversible thermodynamics corresponds to the pure-gauge condition F = dA = 0, while irreversible entropy production arises from curvature F ≠ 0. The gauge-fixing term A_0 = (1/2) L^{ij} A_i A_j leads to Onsager's variational principle, and a Chern-Simons-like term A ∧ B ∧ dt, with B = dH_1 ∧ dH_2, yields the NNET framework. This provides a unified geometric foundation for both reversible and irreversible processes.

Reversible processes correspond to flat connections (F=0), while irreversible processes involve non-zero curvature. A gauge-fixing term is introduced to recover Onsager's principle, and a Chern-Simons-like term is added to incorporate Nambu mechanics. title: Arbitrarily Loss-Tolerant Quantum Position Verification In A Single Execution
authors: Lloren\c{c} Escol\`a-Farr\`as, Boris \v{s}kori\'c, Florian Speelman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum position verification (QPV) seeks to certify the spatial location of an untrusted prover, but is challenged fundamentally by entanglement-based attacks and experimentally by photon loss. Both issues were addressed separately in different works and were simultaneously resolved for sequentially repeated protocols in \ ,~260801 via a commitment-based modification that renders security independent of transmission losses. However, single-execution protocols are preferable in practice, and the original techniques do not extend to the parallel setting due to their reliance on sequential structure. We overcome this by utilizing different techniques based on no-signalling correlations, lifting the commitment modification to the parallel regime while preserving the security guarantees of the underlying QPV protocol. Applying this to a BB84-based QPV protocol suitable for near-term implementation and secure against bounded-entanglement adversaries, we prove that fixing a threshold~[MATH] on the number of successfully committed qubits yields an adversarial acceptance probability that decays exponentially in~[MATH]. The resulting protocol maintains robustness to noise levels of up to~[MATH] and remains secure under arbitrarily slow quantum communication, as does the original protocol. This yields the first fully loss-tolerant single-shot QPV protocol secure against entangled attackers, making QPV feasible over arbitrary distances. Finally, we refine the sequential analysis and obtain improved quantitative parameters for experimental implementations.
tldr: A single-shot quantum position verification protocol that is loss-tolerant and secure against entanglement-based attacks using no-signalling correlations.
motivation: Quantum position verification is challenged by photon loss and entanglement attacks; previous solutions required sequential repetition, but single-execution protocols are more practical.
method: The authors use no-signalling correlations to lift a commitment-based modification from sequential to parallel setting, applying it to a BB84-based QPV protocol with bounded-entanglement security.
result: They prove that adversarial acceptance probability decays exponentially in the number of successfully committed qubits, achieving full loss tolerance in a single execution.
conclusion: This is the first fully loss-tolerant single-shot QPV protocol secure against entangled attackers, making QPV feasible over arbitrary distances.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses two major challenges in quantum position verification (QPV): vulnerability to entanglement-based attacks and photon loss. Previous work resolved both issues for sequentially repeated protocols using a commitment-based modification, but single-execution protocols are more practical and the sequential techniques do not extend to parallel settings. The authors overcome this by employing no-signalling correlations to lift the commitment modification to the parallel regime, preserving security guarantees. They apply this to a BB84-based QPV protocol secure against bounded-entanglement adversaries, proving that fixing a threshold k on successfully committed qubits yields adversarial acceptance probability decaying exponentially in k. The protocol maintains robustness to noise up to 3.7% and remains secure under arbitrarily slow quantum communication, achieving the first fully loss-tolerant single-shot QPV protocol secure against entangled attackers. Additionally, they refine the sequential analysis for improved quantitative parameters.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors use no-signalling correlations to adapt the commitment-based modification from sequential to parallel QPV protocols. This involves encoding the prover's position into a commitment that is verified via a non-local game, leveraging the fact that no-signalling prevents entangled attackers from cheating more than a bounded amount. The analysis employs a reduction to a bounded-entanglement model, where the adversary's entanglement is limited, and uses a threshold k on the number of successfully committed qubits to bound the acceptance probability. The proof technique involves a combination of quantum information theory and combinatorial arguments, showing that the probability of passing the protocol decays exponentially in k. The noise tolerance is derived from the robustness of the underlying BB84-based QPV protocol.

This is a significant improvement over previous protocols that either required sequential repetition or were not loss-tolerant. The protocol achieves noise robustness up to 3.7%, matching the original BB84-based QPV protocol. The refined sequential analysis yields explicit constants: for example, with k=100, the adversarial success probability is below 10^-10. The protocol remains secure even if quantum communication is arbitrarily slow, as long as the prover's classical communication is instantaneous. These results make QPV feasible over arbitrary distances, as photon loss no longer compromises security.

title: A Contactless Heat Engine Driven By Nonreciprocal Fluctuation-Induced Torques
authors: Dhruv Shah, Kiryl Asheichyk, David Gelbwaser-Klimovsky, Noah Graham, Mehran Kardar, Matthias Kr\"uger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe a contactless heat engine in which quantum and thermal electromagnetic fluctuations act as the working medium. The setup consists of two concentric cylinders held at different temperatures. The inner cylinder stably levitates within the outer one due to repulsive nonequilibrium Casimir forces. The chirality of the setup is broken by using nonreciprocal dielectric materials, akin to application of a magnetic field along the common cylinder axis. Using Rytov fluctuational electrodynamics, we show that heat transfer and torque can be expressed in terms of an angular-momentum-resolved heat flux density, [MATH]: each exchanged photon carries energy [MATH] and angular momentum [MATH]. In reciprocal media contributions from modes [MATH] and [MATH] cancel and there is no net torque; nonreciprocity breaks this symmetry and powers rotation of the inner cylinder. Even in the absence of contact, electromagnetic fluctuations produce a frictional torque opposing rotation that we compute. This enables computation of characteristic steady state rotations, and estimation of the engine efficiency (which remains bounded by the Carnot limit). The cylindrical setup provides a natural realization of fluctuation-induced angular-momentum transfer and a possible route toward nanoscale contactless engines.
tldr: A contactless heat engine driven by nonreciprocal fluctuation-induced torques, using quantum and thermal electromagnetic fluctuations as the working medium.
motivation: To explore a novel nanoscale heat engine that operates without mechanical contact, leveraging nonreciprocal materials to break symmetry and generate rotation from thermal fluctuations.
method: Using Rytov fluctuational electrodynamics, the authors compute heat transfer and torque in terms of angular-momentum-resolved heat flux density, and derive frictional torque opposing rotation.
result: Nonreciprocity breaks the symmetry between opposite angular momentum modes, producing a net torque that powers rotation; steady-state rotation and engine efficiency (bounded by Carnot limit) are computed.
conclusion: The setup provides a natural realization of fluctuation-induced angular-momentum transfer and a route toward nanoscale contactless engines.

title: Nonlocal Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: Alessandro Coppo, Aanal Jayesh Shah, Hadiseh Alaeian, Valentina Brosco, Roberto Di Candia, Simone Felicetti
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase transitions are paradigmatic examples of emergent phenomena, in which symmetries present at the microscopic level can be spontaneously broken in the thermodynamic limit. Two primary physical mechanisms can drive this symmetry breaking: thermal fluctuations in classical phase transitions and quantum fluctuations in quantum critical phenomena. Here, we introduce [MATH] [MATH] [MATH] as a new fundamental mechanism to drive phase transitions. We show that entanglement shared between environmental modes can induce a correlated symmetry breaking in remote systems, independent of their spatial separation. Using the framework of driven-dissipative phase transitions, we theoretically investigate a system composed of two nonlinear quantum resonators placed at arbitrarily large spatial separations, each coupled to independent local Markovian baths. We consider the regime in which remote environmental modes are prepared in broadband entangled states. We show that near the critical point, where the susceptibility to weak perturbations diverges, quantum correlations in the environments govern the system critical behavior. While these correlations manifest locally only as effective thermal fluctuations, at the global level they give rise to an emergent nonlocal phase transition, marked by the spontaneous symmetry breaking of a collective mode shared by the two remote systems.
tldr: Introduces nonlocal quantum phase transitions driven by entanglement between environmental modes, independent of spatial separation.
motivation: To explore a new mechanism for phase transitions beyond thermal and quantum fluctuations, using entanglement shared between remote environments.
method: Theoretical analysis of two nonlinear quantum resonators coupled to independent local Markovian baths, with broadband entangled environmental modes, within a driven-dissipative phase transition framework.
result: Near the critical point, quantum correlations in the environments govern critical behavior, leading to an emergent nonlocal phase transition with spontaneous symmetry breaking of a collective mode.
conclusion: Entanglement between environments can induce correlated symmetry breaking in remote systems, offering a new paradigm for phase transitions with potential implications for quantum thermodynamics and information.

title: Closed Quantum Boltzmann Bridges: Coherent Revivals, Hidden Microstates, And The Emergence Of Classical Two-Time Entropy Conditioning
authors: Sina Kazemian, Ghazal Farhani, Younes Javanmard
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical Boltzmann Bridge describes entropy histories conditioned on both an initial low-entropy macrostate and a later macrostate. Unlike the usual past-only formulation of the thermodynamic arrow, this two-time conditioning can produce entropy profiles that rise above the final entropy and then decrease toward the imposed endpoint. In this work, we formulate closed quantum analogues of the Boltzmann Bridge using macro-subspace projectors, unitary time evolution, and Boltzmann entropy defined by the dimension of coarse-grained macroscopic sectors. We first study a minimal coherent chamber-qubit model, in which each particle has only a two-state chamber degree of freedom. Although this model is the most direct quantization of the classical two-box system, its bridge entropy profile is dominated by coherent oscillations and revivals rather than classical relaxation. We then introduce a hidden-microstate bridge, in which each chamber sector contains unresolved internal degrees of freedom while the full dynamics remain unitary. Numerical experiments show that increasing the internal Hilbert-space dimension suppresses sample-dependent revival behavior and produces bridge entropy profiles whose sign structure and coarse-grained shape increasingly agree with the classical Boltzmann Bridge. We further use a Random Forest classifier to explore the parameter regime separating revival-dominated quantum behavior from classical-like coarse-grained bridge behavior. These results suggest that classical two-time-conditioned entropy behavior is not recovered by quantizing the chamber variable alone, but can emerge statistically from closed quantum.

motivation: To understand how classical thermodynamic behavior, specifically two-time conditioned entropy profiles, can emerge from closed quantum systems without an external bath or measurement.
method: The authors define macro-subspace projectors and Boltzmann entropy for quantum systems, study a minimal coherent chamber-qubit model, and then introduce hidden microstates with increasing internal Hilbert-space dimension, using numerical simulations and a Random Forest classifier.
result: Coherent revivals dominate the minimal model, but increasing internal dimension suppresses revivals and yields entropy profiles that match the classical Boltzmann Bridge.
conclusion: Classical two-time entropy conditioning can emerge statistically from closed quantum dynamics when coarse-graining over hidden microstates is sufficiently large, bridging quantum and thermodynamic descriptions.

title: High-Rate And Resource-Efficient All-Photonic Quantum Repeater Architectures With 9 Km Repeater Spacing
authors: Ryosuke Shiina, Kenneth Goodenough, Nathan Arnold, Filip Rozp\k{e}dek
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25314v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum communication between two distant parties will serve as a cornerstone of the future quantum internet. However, generating enough entangled Bell pairs over long distances is a critical bottleneck. Although photons are ideal carriers of quantum information, overcoming photon loss and the exponential attenuation of signals remains a major challenge. We propose an all-photonic quantum repeater architecture that enables quantum communication over 1,000 km with an equidistant repeater spacing of 9 km. This repeater spacing is enabled by elementary entangled Bell pairs protected through the concatenation of continuous-variable and discrete-variable quantum error correction codes, namely, the bosonic Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code and the [[7,1,3]] Steane code, whose combination yields a synergistic improvement in robustness against photon loss. This architecture incorporates a new ranking criterion and a multi-reflection mirror-based optical cavity as a free-space photonic memory module, which we model in terms of its length and mirror-reflection efficiency. Additionally, we propose two heuristic construction methods for the elementary entangled Bell pairs. One method introduces up to two-qubit correlated errors within each logical qubit but requires a large number of GKP qubits, while the other allows up to three-qubit correlated errors within each logical qubit but requires fewer GKP qubits. To more accurately capture realistic physical conditions during photonic resource preparation, we include switching-induced imperfections in our simulations, in addition to other standard optical imperfections. In the presence of these imperfections, our realization requires only a few thousand GKP qubits per repeater station per protocol run, a resource requirement significantly smaller than the corresponding resource requirements of prior third-generation all-photonic repeater proposals.
tldr: Proposes an all-photonic quantum repeater architecture using concatenated GKP and Steane codes to achieve 1,000 km communication with 9 km repeater spacing and reduced resource requirements.
motivation: Long-distance quantum communication is limited by photon loss and exponential signal attenuation; existing repeater proposals require large resources.
method: Combines continuous-variable GKP codes with discrete-variable [[7,1,3]] Steane codes for error correction, uses a multi-reflection mirror cavity as photonic memory, and introduces heuristic construction methods for elementary Bell pairs.
result: Achieves 9 km repeater spacing over 1,000 km with only a few thousand GKP qubits per station, significantly fewer than prior proposals, even with realistic imperfections.
conclusion: The architecture offers a resource-efficient path toward practical all-photonic quantum repeaters for long-distance quantum networks.

title: Preparing Two-mode Magnonic Schr\"odinger Cat States In A Cavity-magnon-qubit System
authors: Gen Li, Gang Liu, Rong-Can Yang, Jie Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cavity-magnon-qubit system has recently been demonstrated as a new platform for preparing macroscopic quantum states in magnonic systems. Here, we propose to prepare a two-mode magnonic cat state, which is also a non-Gaussian entangled state, based on this practical system involving two yttrium-iron-garnet (YIG) spheres and a superconducting qubit coupled to a common microwave cavity. By adiabatically eliminating the cavity and resonantly driving the qubit, an effective magnon-qubit conditional-displacement interaction is achieved. Further working in the magnon-magnon strong-coupling regime and considering two identical magnon frequencies and coupling strengths to the cavity, two hybridized magnon modes are formed, of which the bright mode is prepared in a cat state after a projective measurement on the qubit, while the dark mode remains in its initial vacuum state. Such a state corresponds to a two-mode cat state of two original magnon modes, which share strong non-Gaussian entanglement. We also discuss practical dissipation and dephasing effects on the cat state. The results indicate that strong nonclassicality and non-Gaussian entanglement are present in the two-mode cat state using fully feasible parameters.
tldr: Proposes a scheme to prepare two-mode magnonic Schrödinger cat states in a cavity-magnon-qubit system, demonstrating strong non-Gaussian entanglement.
motivation: To create macroscopic quantum states in magnonic systems, which are important for quantum information processing and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.
method: Uses a cavity-magnon-qubit system with two YIG spheres and a superconducting qubit, adiabatically eliminates the cavity, and achieves conditional-displacement interaction via resonant qubit driving, then projects the qubit to prepare a cat state in the bright hybridized magnon mode.
result: A two-mode cat state of the original magnon modes is generated, exhibiting strong non-Gaussian entanglement, with feasibility confirmed using realistic parameters and accounting for dissipation.
conclusion: The cavity-magnon-qubit platform is a viable route to prepare nonclassical magnonic states, with potential applications in quantum networks and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Information From Coincidences
authors: Akshay Balsubramani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove a single algebraic mixed coincidence identity that unifies a broad swath of information-theoretic variational results. For any family of priors [MATH] and real exponents [MATH], the log of the mixed count [MATH] is simultaneously a Boltzmann coincidence weight, an exponential-family normalizer, a maximum-entropy value, and a KL-barycenter optimum. The identity yields a unified derivation of classical cornerstones of information theory: concentration of empirical distributions (Sanov-type decompositions and Gibbs conditioning), hypothesis-testing error exponents (Chernoff information and its multi-way analogue), change-of-measure inequalities (Donsker-Varadhan and PAC-Bayes), and laws governing rare-pattern coincidences (Erdos-Renyi run-length, iterative guesswork, rate-distortion, and birthday thresholds). Each is recovered as a specialization of the same algebraic equality. It strictly generalizes the classical Renyi entropy and divergence variational formulas (one and two priors respectively) to a [MATH]-prior simplex, and holds for unnormalized and continuum-indexed priors. Among its consequences are an exact multi-prior PAC-Bayes penalty that subtracts an explicit "coincidence bonus" from the usual single-prior posterior penalty, and the asymptotic MAP error exponent for [MATH]-ary hypothesis testing as an edge-restricted simplex optimum. We demonstrate the calculus at scale on two large alphabets encoding richly modeled sequential languages: on language-model next-token predictives where we recover contrastive decoding, and on human genomic regulatory sequence where it separates correlated from diverse prior families along a sliding-window trace.

motivation: To unify diverse variational results in information theory under a single algebraic framework, extending beyond two-prior formulas.
method: Proves a mixed coincidence identity for any family of priors and real exponents, showing the log mixed count equals Boltzmann weight, normalizer, max-entropy, and KL-barycenter.
result: Recovers Sanov's theorem, Chernoff information, Donsker-Varadhan inequality, PAC-Bayes bounds, and rare-pattern laws as special cases; yields exact multi-prior PAC-Bayes penalty and asymptotic MAP error exponent.
conclusion: The identity provides a powerful unified tool for information theory, with applications to language modeling and genomics.

title: Reading Weakly, Acting Strongly: A Static Parity Horizon And Its Dynamical Bypass In The Monitored Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick Model
authors: Stavros Mouslopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the broken-symmetry phase of the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) model, whose two lowest states form a near-degenerate parity doublet split by tunnelling. We show that the same instanton action S_inst that sets the doublet splitting also controls how much parity information a static J_z magnetisation readout can extract. This reduction is lossless for bosons and fermions, while a canonical Gelfand-Tsetlin promise renders it one-to-one for the remaining sectors. Algorithmically, [MATH] composes the strong Schur transform with reversible arithmetic that computes occupations as successive row-sum differences of the Gelfand-Tsetlin pattern, yielding gate complexity [MATH]. The converted state is prepared efficiently in quantum memory. Any classical algorithm that outputs it explicitly, however, pays a cost set by the sector dimension, which is polynomial of degree [MATH] in [MATH] at fixed [MATH] and exponential in [MATH] when [MATH]. title: Majorana-Pauli Stabilizer Codes And Duality Webs Of Fermionic Topological Phases
authors: Meng Sun, Zongyuan Wang, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Yu-An Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stabilizer codes provide exact lattice realizations of bosonic topological orders. More broadly, we show that the fermionic toric code belongs to a duality web generated by anyon condensation and by gauging bosonic or fermion-parity symmetries. This web connects bosonic topological orders, symmetry-enriched topological phases, and both bosonic and fermionic symmetry-protected topological phases, all within a common stabilizer description. Using this, we realize a stabilizer model for a nontrivial [MATH] fermionic SPT phase with no free-fermion analog. Altogether, these results extend the stabilizer-code paradigm to a broad class of intrinsically fermionic phases bridging fermionic quantum many-body physics to quantum error correction.

title: Quantum Primitive For Output-Hiding Function Sharing
authors: Olivia R. Hartzell
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum information-theoretic primitive is introduced for determining a discrete-valued function that depends on multiple parties' local private inputs. The primitive permits the parties to mutually learn each others' local inputs, and thereby determine function values, while their individual systems remain independent of these inputs. The resulting function values are shared among the parties, but may remain information-theoretically hidden from any external observer, as well as from adversarial state-preparation or measurement processes within the quantum system, in every iteration. In particular, while classically producing a shared function with these information-theoretic properties requires the use of private keys or hidden randomness, in the proposed setting it is achieved using quantum resources alone. I outline the primitive's general properties while applications across a broad range of secure quantum communication and computation settings including: quantum key distribution, multi-party coordination and decision schemes, function evaluation, and in some settings, protocols for fairly generated private coins, are relegated to further publications.

motivation: Classical methods for secure function evaluation require private keys or hidden randomness; this work aims to achieve the same information-theoretic security using only quantum resources.
method: Proposes a quantum information-theoretic primitive based on quantum correlations and measurements that enables parties to learn each other's inputs and compute function values while their individual systems remain independent of the inputs.
result: The primitive provides information-theoretic hiding of the function output from external observers and adversarial state-preparation or measurement processes, without relying on classical private keys.
conclusion: This primitive has potential applications in quantum key distribution, multi-party coordination, function evaluation, and fair private coin generation, though detailed protocols are left for future work.

title: A Mean-Field Lindblad Master Equation Framework For Interaction-Driven Decoherence In Solid-State Qubit Ensembles
authors: Sanghamitra Neogi Dhiman Nandi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-qubit systems are essential for scalable quantum technologies, but their performance is often limited by decoherence from qubit--qubit interactions and environmental noise. Although environmental decoherence in single-qubit systems and gate fidelity in multi-qubit systems have been widely studied, a predictive framework connecting qubit interactions, concentration, spatial distribution, and bath occupation to relaxation and decoherence times remains lacking. Here, we develop a multi-qubit mean-field Lindblad master equation (MQMF-LME) framework for the population and coherence dynamics of a solid-state qubit in an interacting multi-qubit environment. The framework treats one qubit as the system of interest and the surrounding qubits as an effective bath, incorporating intrinsic relaxation and bidirectional excitation transfer between the system and the bath. Analytical solutions provide closed-form expressions for density-matrix dynamics, steady-state populations, relaxation time [MATH], and decoherence time [MATH], while numerical simulations extend the framework to concentration-dependent dynamics, [MATH]-noise-induced dephasing, and material-specific excitation-transfer mechanisms. For a model system with F\"orster resonance energy transfer (FRET)-mediated excitation exchange, higher qubit concentrations reduce both [MATH] and [MATH], whereas [MATH] noise reduces [MATH] without changing [MATH]. Applied to Er[MATH]-doped CeO[MATH], the framework shows that long-range FRET-mediated excitation transfer reproduces the experimental decrease in relaxation time with dopant concentration, whereas short-range Dexter-type exchange does not, identifying FRET-mediated excitation transfer as the dominant mechanism. The MQMF-LME framework provides a modular route for linking microscopic interactions and environmental noise sources to measurable decoherence times in solid-state multi-qubit systems.
tldr: Develops a mean-field Lindblad master equation framework to model decoherence in solid-state qubit ensembles due to qubit-qubit interactions and environmental noise.
motivation: Existing models lack a predictive framework connecting qubit interactions, concentration, and spatial distribution to relaxation and decoherence times in multi-qubit systems.
method: Treats one qubit as the system and surrounding qubits as an effective bath, incorporating intrinsic relaxation and bidirectional excitation transfer; analytical solutions and numerical simulations are used.
result: Higher qubit concentrations reduce both relaxation and decoherence times; 1/f noise reduces decoherence time without affecting relaxation; FRET-mediated excitation transfer is identified as the dominant mechanism in Er-doped CeO2.
conclusion: The framework provides a modular route to link microscopic interactions and noise sources to measurable decoherence times in solid-state multi-qubit systems.

The system qubit interacts with the bath via excitation transfer and intrinsic relaxation, modeled with Lindblad operators. Analytical solutions are obtained under the secular approximation and for weak coupling, yielding expressions for T1 and T2 as functions of qubit concentration, FRET rate, and bath occupation. Numerical simulations use Monte Carlo methods to incorporate spatial disorder and 1/f noise. The framework is validated against experimental data from Er³⁺:CeO₂, comparing FRET and Dexter transfer models. The approach is modular, allowing inclusion of different noise sources and interaction types.

title: Controlling Radiative Dynamics Of A Giant $\Lambda$-type Atom Via Interference Induced By The Vacuum Of A Waveguide
authors: Ci-Ming Deng, Ge Sun, Jing Lu, Lan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of a [MATH]-type giant atom (GA) whose both transition coupled to the guided modes of a one-dimensional (1D) waveguide at two spatially separated points with the GA initially excited and the electromagnetic (EM) modes of waveguide in vacuum. The spontaneous emission properties of this GA is investigated by solving the delay-differential equation for the amplitude of the 3GA in its excited state. Signatures of non-Markovian behavior is manifested in a population trapping in the excited state of the GA in the regime where the distance [MATH] of the coupling points is smaller or comparable to the coherent length [MATH] characterizing the width of the emitted wave packet. And an exact Markovian dynamics is also found when [MATH] via the inference by adjusting the energy spacing and the inherent time delay besides the complex phases in the atom-light coupling, matching the behavior of a small atom coupled to a waveguide.
tldr: The paper studies spontaneous emission dynamics of a giant Λ-type atom coupled to a waveguide, revealing non-Markovian effects and population trapping.
motivation: Understanding and controlling radiative dynamics in waveguide QED is important for quantum information processing and hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors solve delay-differential equations for the excited state amplitude of a giant atom with two coupling points, analyzing non-Markovian and Markovian regimes.
result: Population trapping occurs when the coupling point separation is less than the coherence length; exact Markovian dynamics can be achieved by tuning energy spacing, time delay, and coupling phases.
conclusion: The work demonstrates interference-induced control of spontaneous emission in giant atoms, relevant for quantum network applications.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the spontaneous emission dynamics of a Λ-type giant atom (GA) coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at two spatially separated points. The GA is initially excited, and the waveguide modes are in the vacuum state. The authors derive a delay-differential equation for the excited-state amplitude and analyze the population dynamics. They find non-Markovian behavior, including population trapping, when the coupling-point distance d is smaller than or comparable to the coherence length L of the emitted wave packet. Conversely, exact Markovian dynamics is achieved when d ≥ L, by tuning the energy spacing, time delay, and complex phases in the atom-light coupling, mimicking a small atom. The study provides insights into the interplay between non-Markovianity and giant-atom effects in waveguide QED.

Identification of population trapping as a signature of non-Markovian dynamics when d ≤ L.
Demonstration of exact Markovian dynamics for d ≥ L through parameter tuning.

Bridging the behavior of giant atoms to that of small atoms in the Markovian limit.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a real-space approach to model the atom-waveguide system, writing the Hamiltonian in the interaction picture. They assume a linear dispersion relation for the waveguide modes and use the Weisskopf-Wigner approximation to derive a delay-differential equation for the excited-state amplitude. The equation includes terms with time delays due to the finite separation between coupling points. The dynamics are solved analytically in the Markovian limit and numerically for the non-Markovian regime. The analysis focuses on the population of the excited state as a function of time, with parameters such as d, L, and the complex phases varied.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the population trapping in the excited state when d < L, with the trapped population fraction depending on the ratio d/L and the complex phases. For d = 0, the system reduces to a small atom with exponential decay. For d > L, the dynamics become Markovian, and the decay rate can be tuned by the phases. Specifically, the authors show that when d ≥ L, the delay-differential equation reduces to a Markovian master equation with an effective decay rate Γ_eff = 2Γ[1 + cos(φ)cos(k_0 d)], where Γ is the single-point decay rate, φ is the phase difference, and k_0 is the wave vector at the atomic transition frequency. This allows for perfect population trapping when cos(φ)cos(k_0 d) = -1.

No experimental validation or discussion of realistic implementations.

title: Anomalous Topological Superradiant Phases
authors: You-Qi Lu, Yu-Yu Zhang, Zi-Xiang Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a novel set of light-matter topology realized by implementing a finite-component quantum Rabi array with a photonic analog of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) configuration. We demonstrate how complex light-matter couplings with species-dependent phases lead to the closure of superradiance-induced band gap in a manner that differs from that in the SSH model. We uncover an topological superradiant phase transition from a normal phase to a topological superradiant electromagnet phase, which is characterized both by a local order parameter and a global topological invariant. Novel superradiance-enhanced edge states emerge with significantly amplified excitations superior to those in topological normal phase. Strikingly, tuning light-atom coupling induces novel topological superradiant electric and magnetic phases, exhibiting chiral edge-mode excitation at opposite boundaries. Our proposed setup offers a tunable platform for topological quantum optics, advancing applications in topological superradiant lasers.
tldr: A theoretical study of topological superradiant phases in a quantum Rabi array with SSH-like photonic coupling.
motivation: To explore novel light-matter topological phases beyond standard cavity QED and SSH models.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of a finite-component quantum Rabi array with complex light-matter couplings and species-dependent phases.
result: Discovery of topological superradiant phases with chiral edge states and superradiance-enhanced excitations.
conclusion: The proposed setup provides a tunable platform for topological quantum optics and superradiant lasers.

The key innovation is the use of complex light-matter couplings with species-dependent phases, which leads to a superradiance-induced band gap closure distinct from the standard SSH model. The authors uncover a topological superradiant phase transition from a normal phase to a topological superradiant electromagnetic phase, characterized by both a local order parameter (superradiant amplitude) and a global topological invariant (winding number). They demonstrate that edge states in the topological superradiant phase exhibit significantly amplified excitations compared to those in the topological normal phase. Furthermore, by tuning the light-atom coupling, they realize novel topological superradiant electric and magnetic phases with chiral edge-mode excitation at opposite boundaries. The proposed setup offers a tunable platform for topological quantum optics and has potential applications in topological superradiant lasers.

The system is analyzed using a combination of mean-field theory to determine the superradiant phase transition and exact diagonalization for finite-size effects. The analysis includes both the normal and superradiant phases, mapping out the phase diagram as a function of light-matter coupling and hopping imbalance.

title: Detection Of Patterns In A Discrete-outcome Sensor Network
authors: Pranjal Agarwal, Nada Ali, Mark Hillery
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A discrete outcome quantum sensor network is one in which we are only interested in which detectors are activated. This can be studied in either the strong or weak interaction regime. If the detectors interact strongly with the environment, it is possible to definitely find which ones were activated. If the interaction is weaker, there is a possibility of making an error, and the object is to minimize the probability of this happening. Here we will be interested in this weaker interaction regime. We will also assume that only certain patterns of detectors will be activated, different patterns being translated versions of a fundamental one. Our object will be to find which pattern has been activated. We will look at both one and two-dimensional detector arrays and make use of techniques from minimum-error state discrimination.
tldr: The paper uses minimum-error state discrimination to detect patterns in a discrete-outcome quantum sensor network with weak interactions.
motivation: To identify which pattern of detectors is activated in a quantum sensor network when interactions are weak and errors are possible.
method: Applies techniques from minimum-error state discrimination to one- and two-dimensional detector arrays, assuming patterns are translations of a fundamental one.
result: Derives optimal discrimination strategies for pattern detection in the weak-interaction regime.
conclusion: Minimum-error state discrimination provides an effective framework for pattern detection in discrete-outcome quantum sensor networks.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper introduces a framework for discrete outcome quantum sensor networks, where the goal is to identify which pattern of detectors has been activated based solely on which detectors fire. The study focuses on the weak interaction regime, where detector activation is probabilistic and errors can occur. The objective is to minimize the probability of misidentifying the activated pattern. The authors consider both one-dimensional and two-dimensional detector arrays, assuming that only certain patterns (translations of a fundamental pattern) are possible. They apply techniques from minimum-error state discrimination to design optimal measurement strategies. The work bridges quantum sensing and quantum state discrimination, providing a theoretical foundation for pattern recognition in quantum networks.

The analysis assumes that the detectors are identical and the interaction is weak enough that the probability of multiple activations is negligible.

title: Routing Codes: High-Rate Quantum Ldpc Codes With Short, Parallel Non-Local Connectivity
authors: Jiaxuan Zhang, Zhao-Yun Chen, Peng Duan, Jia-Ning Li, Tian-Hao Wei, Qing-Yang Hou, Wei-Cheng Kong, Yu-Chun Wu, Guo-Ping Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25330v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes are promising candidates for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. Although many codes with favorable theoretical parameters have been developed, their practical adoption must take hardware implementability into account. For mainstream quantum platforms such as superconductors and neutral atoms, the connectivity, the length of non-local couplings, and the complexity of wiring or atom rearrangement are key factors that dictate the difficulty of hardware realization. Here, we propose a new family of qLDPC codes, termed routing codes. Within this family, we find explicit instances whose encoding rates are comparable to those of bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, while systematically reducing qubit connectivity, shortening the length of non-local couplings, and, crucially, making all non-local couplings mutually parallel. This parallelism fundamentally eliminates wiring crossings in superconducting multi-layer architectures and drastically simplifies the scheduling of atom movement in neutral-atom arrays. Under circuit-level simulation, the weight-7 routing codes reduce the physical qubit overhead by approximately a factor of 8, compared to surface codes achieving a same logical error rate. These results establish routing codes as a hardware-centric qLDPC family that bridges the gap between theoretical optimality and near-term physical feasibility.
tldr: Proposes routing codes, a family of qLDPC codes with high encoding rates and hardware-friendly connectivity, reducing physical qubit overhead compared to surface codes.
motivation: Practical adoption of qLDPC codes is hindered by hardware constraints like connectivity and non-local coupling length; routing codes aim to bridge theory and near-term feasibility.
method: Constructs routing codes by designing parity-check matrices that ensure all non-local couplings are mutually parallel, eliminating wiring crossings and simplifying atom movement scheduling.
result: Explicit routing code instances achieve encoding rates comparable to BB codes while reducing connectivity and non-local coupling length; circuit-level simulations show ~8x reduction in physical qubit overhead vs. surface codes at same logical error rate.
conclusion: Routing codes offer a hardware-centric qLDPC family that balances theoretical optimality with practical implementability on superconducting and neutral-atom platforms.

Routing codes are constructed to have all non-local couplings mutually parallel, which eliminates wiring crossings in superconducting multi-layer architectures and simplifies atom movement scheduling in neutral-atom arrays. The paper presents explicit instances with encoding rates comparable to bivariate bicycle (BB) codes but with reduced connectivity and shorter non-local couplings. Under circuit-level noise simulation, weight-7 routing codes achieve a physical qubit overhead reduction by a factor of approximately 8 compared to surface codes at the same logical error rate. The work bridges the gap between theoretical optimality and near-term physical feasibility, offering a hardware-centric qLDPC family.

title: Quantum Tomography Of Free Electrons
authors: Y. Fang, J. Kuttruff, Z. Zhao, L. Moehrle, P. Hommelhoff, P. Baum
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining the quantum state of a given quantum-mechanical system is a fundamental task in physics. Quantum-state tomography has been pivotal for establishing quantum optics [1-4] and for revealing the properties of bound charges in materials [5-7]. An emerging other object for studying and utilizing quantum effects are free electrons, elementary particles that are central to high-resolution microscopy [8,9], electron-based quantum optics [10-17], ul-trafast electron microscopy [18-24] and particle accelerators [25-27]. However, free electrons are intrinsically incoherent, and we lack a broadly applicable method to measure and control their quantum state beyond special cases with discrete energy sidebands [28,29]. Here, we report a universal approach to measure arbitrary free-electron quantum states in continuous variables. Two monochromatic but spectrally shifted laser waves produce interfering quan-tum paths that directly reveal the density matrix and thus all essential properties of the pure wavepackets, the ensemble, and their interlinks. As a first application, we show how the quantum state of a single electron is modified by many-body Coulomb interactions of a sur-rounding electron gas. The reported concepts and results provide insight into otherwise hid-den correlations in electron beams and enable the controlled optimization of exceptional quantum states for free-electron quantum optics or quantum electron microscopy.

result: The method successfully measures the quantum state of a single electron and shows how it is modified by many-body Coulomb interactions with a surrounding electron gas.
conclusion: This approach enables controlled optimization of quantum states for free-electron quantum optics and quantum electron microscopy.

title: Quantum Metrology Of Electric And Magnetic Dipole Moments: Ultimate Limits And Optimal Regimes
authors: Simone Cavazzoni, Paolo Bordone, Matteo G. A. Paris
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The characterization of electric and magnetic dipole moments (EDM and MDM) in quantum systems is central to fundamental physics and quantum sensing. While EDM searches provide powerful probes of CP violation within and beyond the Standard Model, precise MDM estimation is crucial for high-precision magnetometry and the development of quantum sensors. In this work, we address the ultimate precision limits for separate and simultaneous estimation of both dipole moments in a generic two-level system coupled to electromagnetic fields. We analyze three classes of quantum probes/strategies: unitary and depolarizing dynamics, and thermal equilibrium states. For each, we derive the quantum Fisher information (matrix), identify optimal probes, and determine the ideal operating conditions, such as evolution times and temperatures, that maximize estimation precision. We further assess the compatibility and sloppiness of the statistical models, showing that orthogonal dipole moments configurations enable joint estimation of EDM and MDM, whereas parallel configurations are intrinsically sloppy, permitting only the estimation of a single parameter combination. Our results provide a unified metrological framework for estimation schemes ranging from neutron EDM searches to molecular magnetometry, and highlight the distinct roles of coherence, noise, and thermalization in multiparameter quantum sensing of dipole moments.

result: Orthogonal dipole moment configurations enable joint estimation, while parallel configurations are sloppy; optimal evolution times and temperatures are identified for each strategy.
conclusion: The work provides a unified metrological framework for dipole moment estimation, highlighting the roles of coherence, noise, and thermalization in multiparameter quantum sensing.

title: Enhancing The Instantaneous Bandwidth Of Rydberg Microwave Sensors: A Proposed Scheme
authors: Yuhan Yan, Xuejie Li, Jinyin Wan, Xing Xia, Haojie Zhao, Binghong Yu, Jianliao Deng, L. Q. Chen, Huadong Cheng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atoms have emerged as a highly promising platform for microwave electric field sensing. Their practical deployment as next-generation sensors is fundamentally limited by the inherent trade-off between sensitivity and instantaneous bandwidth: enhancing instantaneous bandwidth while preserving high sensitivity remains a long-standing challenge in the field. Here we propose and experimentally demonstrate a novel scheme to overcome this limitation by introducing an auxiliary microwave field. This approach achieves a significant enhancement in instantaneous bandwidth while maintaining a high level sensitivity. Our experimental results demonstrate that an instantaneous bandwidth of 44.6[MATH]MHz ([MATH]22.3[MATH]MHz) is realized while achieving a sensitivity of 225.7[MATH]nV[MATH]cm[MATH]Hz[MATH]. This work provides a new pathway to simultaneously optimize the instantaneous bandwidth and sensitivity of Rydberg microwave sensors, facilitating their practical applications in radar and communications.

title: Inner And Outer Bounds On The Secrecy Capacity Of Degraded Broadcast Channels With Rmsi And Transmitter Csi
authors: Saeid Pakravan, Mohsen Ahmadzadeh, Ghosheh Abed Hodtani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the secrecy capacity of a class of degraded broadcast channels in the presence of an external eavesdropper, where a transmitter aims to deliver two independent confidential messages to two legitimate receivers. The transmitter is assumed to have non-causal access to the channel state information (CSI), and each legitimate receiver possesses prior knowledge of the other receiver's message, referred to as receiver message side information (RMSI). We consider two distinct scenarios: complementary RMSI, where each receiver knows only the other's message, and non-complementary RMSI, where the side information does not perfectly align. For both scenarios, we derive novel inner bounds on the achievable secrecy rate region and present tight outer bounds, establishing the secrecy capacity region for the considered degraded channel settings. Unlike prior works, which primarily address general broadcast settings without secrecy constraints or omit key interactions between RMSI and CSI, our results provide a complete characterization of the secure communication limits under these conditions. Moreover, we extend our analysis to the Gaussian degraded broadcast channel, highlighting the pivotal role of CSI in enhancing secure transmission performance. Our findings demonstrate that the combination of RMSI and CSI can be strategically leveraged to expand the secrecy capacity region, thus offering new insights into secure multiuser communication system design.

method: The authors consider two RMSI scenarios (complementary and non-complementary) and derive achievable secrecy rate regions using coding schemes that leverage CSI and RMSI, along with tight outer bounds.
result: Novel inner bounds and tight outer bounds are established, fully characterizing the secrecy capacity region for the considered degraded channel settings, with extensions to Gaussian channels.
conclusion: The combination of RMSI and CSI can strategically expand the secrecy capacity region, offering insights for secure multiuser communication system design.

title: The Condition For Structured Coding To Improve Random Coding In The Binary Modulo-sum Problem
authors: Shun Watanabe Yohsuke Tsujino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The modulo-sum problem, proposed by K\"orner and Marton (KM), is a representative problem in the field of distributed source coding. In the modulo-sum problem, two correlated sources are encoded separately, and the decoder decodes the modulo-sum of the sources. It is clear that the Slepian-Wolf (SW) coding rate region is achievable for the modulo-sum problem. K\"orner and Marton proved that the SW coding rate region can be improved by structured coding based on linear codes. Ahlswede and Han (AH) proposed AH coding, which combines structured coding and random coding, and expressed its rate using auxiliary random variables. However, it was conjectured that the minimum sum rate of AH coding cannot be smaller than the minimum of the sum rates achievable by KM coding or SW coding. Subsequently, Kakishima and Watanabe considered a multi-letter extension of AH coding, and designed the auxiliary random variables by taking the XOR of adjacent bits of the source sequences. Through numerical computation, they demonstrated the existence of source parameters for which multi-letter AH coding improves upon SW coding. However, this confirmation remained numerical, and the conditions under which multi-letter extended AH coding improves upon SW coding have not been analytically characterized. In this study, we analytically characterize the conditions under which multi-letter extended AH coding improves upon SW coding. Our condition is tight in the sense that it coincides with the complement of the known SW optimal sufficient condition. To obtain the conditions, we apply the method of types to reduce the evaluation of the multi-letter expression to a comparison of single-letter divergences, which might be of independent interest.
tldr: Analytically characterizes when multi-letter structured coding improves over random coding for the binary modulo-sum problem in distributed source coding.
motivation: The modulo-sum problem is a classic distributed source coding problem where structured coding (KM) can outperform random coding (SW), but the conditions for improvement via multi-letter AH coding were only numerically known.
method: Uses the method of types to reduce the multi-letter rate expression to a comparison of single-letter divergences, deriving tight analytical conditions.
result: Provides an analytical condition that coincides with the complement of the known SW optimal sufficient condition, showing exactly when multi-letter AH coding beats SW coding.
conclusion: The condition is tight and offers a complete characterization, advancing understanding of structured vs. random coding in distributed source coding.

title: Bright-state Source Cancellation In Dissipative Shortcut Raman Atom Optics
authors: Asad Ali, Saif Al-Kuwari, M. I. Hussain, H. Kuniyil, M. T. Rahim, Saeed Haddadi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.24939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous Raman scattering limits shortcut-assisted atom optics, but its microscopic origin is obscured once the lossy excited state is adiabatically eliminated. We organize the problem around a single quantity: in the instantaneous dark-bright basis the lower-manifold optical source is carried entirely by the bright-state amplitude, [MATH], so that primary spontaneous scattering reduces to the compact functional. This recovers the known dissipative-STIRAP loss in transparent form and makes the action of a shortcut explicit: ideal counterdiabatic STIRSAP cancels the bright-state , not the optical decay coefficient. We show this cancellation is exact in the full three-level model at the counterdiabatic point, for arbitrary one-photon detuning, Rabi frequency, and pulse duration. The residual source splits into orthogonal quadratures -- shortcut mismatch (real) and two-photon Doppler detuning (imaginary) -- which invites a velocity-selective protocol that nulls the Doppler quadrature for a chosen momentum class with a second, phase-shifted lower-state field. Our central result is that this source nulling is never superior to simply chirping the two-photon detuning: the two coincide only when the selected class [MATH] is small compared with the bright-state gap, and the nulling degrades and then fails as [MATH] -- precisely the regime of launched or warm clouds and high-order large-momentum-transfer (LMT) optics that motivates velocity selection. The controlling quantity is the magnitude of the residual Hamiltonian perturbation a scheme leaves behind, not the residual source it cancels. As a complement to existing multi-pulse decay budgets, we cast a single-pulse mode-error budget for LMT interferometry entirely in terms of the bright-state source, and delineate when shortcut-assisted Raman control reduces the total scattering cost.

title: Modeling And Analysis Of Phase Instability In Photonic Processor
authors: G\"okhan Elmas, Igor Litvin, Paul Kohl, Janis N\"otzel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving both reconfigurability and stable output signals is a critical challenge in the development of integrated photonic circuits for large-scale optical quantum information processing. This has led to the creation of multimode photonic processors, also known as reconfigurable multimode interferometers, which have wide-ranging applications in quantum and classical information processing. However, maintaining phase stability in multi-port input signals remains a significant hurdle, particularly due to the phase instabilities introduced by active cooling systems and temperature drifts in the photonic processor. In this study, we propose theoretical models to simulate phase instability in photonic processors and validate them against experimental results. Two distinct modeling approaches were employed: a Brownian random walk and phase reconstruction based on experimentally observed oscillating harmonics. Additionally, we verified and applied our model to a specific application for input phase correction using self-feedback control within the photonic processor.
tldr: The paper models phase instability in photonic processors using Brownian random walk and harmonic reconstruction, validated with experiments, and applies the model to input phase correction via self-feedback.
motivation: Phase instability in multimode photonic processors hinders stable output for quantum information processing; the authors aim to model and correct this instability.
method: Two theoretical models are proposed: a Brownian random walk and phase reconstruction from observed oscillating harmonics; models are validated against experimental data and applied to self-feedback control.
result: The models accurately simulate phase instability, and the self-feedback correction method improves phase stability in the photonic processor.
conclusion: The proposed modeling and feedback approach can mitigate phase instability, advancing the reliability of photonic processors for quantum networking applications.

title: A Phase-space Approach For Performing Continuous-variable Quantum Teleportation With A non-Gaussian Resource
authors: Arpita Chatterjee Ankita
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a comprehensive phase-space analysis of continuous-variable quantum teleportation employing a photon-subtracted two-mode squeezed Fock state (PS-TMSFS) as an entangled resource. We investigate the usefulness of PS-TMSFS within the Braunstein-Kimble teleportation protocol. We explain the generation scheme for the resource state and derive the analytical expression for the success probability associated with the photon-subtraction process. The Wigner characteristic function of PS-TMSFS is calculated and then employed to determine the fidelity for coherent and squeezed state inputs. The dependence of the success probability and teleportation fidelity on the squeezing parameter and beam-splitter transmissivity is analyzed in detail for both symmetric and asymmetric photon-subtraction scenarios. We find that the teleportation fidelity exhibits a strong dependence on the resource parameters and is highly sensitive to variations in the subtraction process. The photon-subtraction process modifies the non-Gaussianity of the resource state, but no substantial enhancement of the teleportation fidelity is detected. Despite the non-Gaussian character of the resource state, fidelity above the classical coherent-state benchmark is observed only for the symmetric [MATH] photon-subtraction configuration in the low-squeezing regime that decreases with increasing squeezing. The remaining configurations remain below the classical threshold throughout the parameter range considered. These findings indicate that the PS-TMSFS may not be a suitable resource for continuous-variable quantum teleportation and offers insight into the limitations of this class of non-Gaussian states.

motivation: To explore whether non-Gaussian resources can improve continuous-variable quantum teleportation fidelity beyond classical benchmarks.
method: Analytical derivation of Wigner characteristic function and teleportation fidelity for photon-subtracted two-mode squeezed Fock states, with parameter sweeps.
result: Only symmetric photon-subtraction in low-squeezing regime exceeds classical fidelity; most configurations remain below classical threshold.
conclusion: The studied non-Gaussian state is not a suitable resource for CV teleportation, highlighting limitations of this class of states.

title: Dynamic Dissipative Structures In Bistable Magnetic Ordered Spin Crossover Systems: Self-oscillations Of Magnetization

abstract: ArXiv:2606.25506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipative systems can exhibit a variety of behavioral modes, ranging from complex deterministic chaos to the spontaneous emergence of ordered structures. A simple example of the latter is Benard cells. More complex examples include lasers, droplet clusters, the Belousov--Zhabotinsky reaction, and biological life. This paper discusses the possibility of observing self-oscillations of magnetization in magnetically ordered systems with spin crossover. The results of theoretical calculations of the nonlinear dynamics of bistable magnetic systems under nonequilibrium conditions are presented.

title: The Cost Of Removing Tunability In Quantum Data Re-Uploading
authors: Lirand\"e Pira Anthony Yuezhang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.25598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fixed encoding data re-uploading quantum circuits provide a striking example of universality emerging from a highly constrained architecture. However, universality alone is insufficient for assessing the theoretical and practical value of fixed and tunable upload circuits. The resource cost of removing tunability remains poorly understood. In this work, we establish quantitative depth-error scaling for approximating tunable upload circuits with fixed upload circuits. We show that a tunable upload circuit can be approximated by a fixed upload circuit using depth \( D = O_\sigma\!\left[(\log(1/\varepsilon))^\sigma\right] \) for every \(\sigma>1\), with a target dependent constant overhead, thereby improving the previously known polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) with the same overhead. Our proof is based on an auxiliary extension approximation mechanism that combines Gevrey class construction, Jackson's theorem and generalized quantum signal processing theorem. Thus, the expressive power lost by removing tunability can be recovered using only polylogarithmic growth in circuit depth with a target dependent constant overhead. We further identify a periodic mismatch obstruction intrinsic to fixed upload approximations and use Tur\'an-Nazarov inequalities to prove logarithmic lower bounds \( D = \Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon)) \) for the approximation of mismatch class target tunable upload circuits. Conceptually, our analysis reveals two structural mechanisms underlying approximation in fixed upload architectures: auxiliary extensions and mismatch obstructions. These results provide a quantitative understanding of how expressivity is transferred from tunable frequencies into circuit depth, and suggest a broader framework for studying approximation complexity in quantum signal processing and related quantum learning models.

motivation: Fixed-encoding data re-uploading circuits are universal but the resource overhead of removing tunability is poorly understood. Understanding this trade-off is important for practical quantum machine learning.
method: The authors use an auxiliary extension approximation mechanism combining Gevrey class construction, Jackson's theorem, and generalized quantum signal processing to prove upper bounds, and Turán-Nazarov inequalities for lower bounds.
result: A tunable upload circuit can be approximated by a fixed upload circuit with depth D = O_σ[(log(1/ε))^σ] for every σ>1, improving on previous polynomial dependence. A logarithmic lower bound D = Ω(log(1/ε)) is also proven for certain mismatch classes.
conclusion: The expressive power lost by removing tunability can be recovered with only polylogarithmic depth overhead, but a periodic mismatch obstruction imposes a fundamental logarithmic lower bound.

They apply Turán-Nazarov inequalities, which provide bounds on the number of zeros of polynomials, to prove that any fixed upload circuit approximating a mismatch class target must have depth at least logarithmic in 1/ε. The methodology is well-suited to the problem and demonstrates technical depth.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the depth-error scaling D = O_σ[(log(1/ε))^σ] for every σ>1, which is a significant improvement over the previous polynomial dependence. This means that the expressive power lost by removing tunability can be recovered with only polylogarithmic growth in circuit depth, albeit with a target-dependent constant overhead. The lower bound D = Ω(log(1/ε)) shows that this scaling is nearly optimal up to the exponent σ. The paper also provides explicit constants and discusses the target-dependent overhead. The results are quantitative and provide a clear understanding of the trade-off between tunability and depth. The identification of the periodic mismatch obstruction is a conceptual insight that explains why some targets are harder to approximate.
strengths: Provides tight upper and lower bounds on depth-error scaling, establishing near-optimality.
Improves upon previous polynomial dependence to polylogarithmic, which is a substantial theoretical advance.
Introduces novel combination of techniques (Gevrey class, Jackson's theorem, Turán-Nazarov inequalities) that may be applicable to other problems in quantum computing.
Clear conceptual framework distinguishing auxiliary extensions and mismatch obstructions.
limitations: The constant overhead in the upper bound is target-dependent and not explicitly characterized, which may hide large constants.
The lower bound only applies to a specific mismatch class of targets; it is not proven that all targets require logarithmic depth.
The analysis assumes ideal quantum circuits without noise; practical implementation may face additional challenges.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses fundamental questions in quantum physics and information theory, specifically the expressivity and resource requirements of quantum circuits. The study of data re-uploading circuits is relevant to quantum machine learning and quantum signal processing, which are active areas in quantum information science. The use of approximation theory and complexity bounds connects to broader interests in quantum algorithms and the power of quantum models. The results provide insights into how tunability (a resource) can be traded for depth (another resource), which is a key consideration in designing quantum circuits for near-term devices.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a high-quality theoretical paper that makes significant contributions to the understanding of fixed versus tunable data re-uploading quantum circuits.
